articles.title: UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran
articles.summary: ‘Situation cannot become new normal’, says UN’s Khaled Khiari, as Iran reports three more vessels hitting mines.
articles.body:
At least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out in February, according to the United Nations.

Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, gave the figures , which cover the period up to November 11, during a UN Security Council briefing on Friday.

“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” said Khiari, urging the “full restoration of maritime navigation in the region”.

He pointed out that security incidents in and around Hormuz have been rising, with October recording the highest tally since the start of the conflict.

The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) tracked 136 security incidents involving vessels in Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11. It said 35 of those incidents came in October and 10 in November.

“Every day brings new reports of maritime incidents,” said Khiari. “These incidents are unacceptable,” he added. “Civilian vessels and commercial shipping must not become targets.”

His remarks come as Iranian authorities on Saturday reported that three oil tankers had hit mines while travelling through “unauthorised” or “restricted” areas of Hormuz, catching fire.

Tehran has warned vessels that they must receive Iranian approval to cross the waterway during the conflict, and has repeatedly attacked ships accused of violating its protocol.

“Any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines,” Iran’s navy warned in a statement carried by the country’s IRIB broadcaster.

Iranian officials have insisted the strait will not be open until the US meets its demands , which include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

The US military claims it has cleared the strait’s main routes of mines and that the waterway is open for commercial shipping.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

Khiari, in his remarks to the UN Security Council, said “the present maritime arrangements in the Middle East remain costly, unpredictable, and unsafe”.

“Disruptions to maritime navigation continue to have significant global economic consequences, driving up energy, transport and insurance costs, fuelling inflation and threatening food security amid severely constrained fertiliser shipments.”

articles.title: In 2015, Arizona engineers buried geogrid beneath a forest road; five years later, reinforced sections had no ruts or potholes, while untreated soil deteriorated
articles.summary: Discover how an innovative geogrid technology has successfully reinforced a forest road in Arizona, preventing ruts and potholes over five years, while untreated soil deteriorated significantly.
articles.body: Anyone who has bounced along a rough country road would probably know how fast mud, ruts and potholes can ruin a journey. Engineers in northern Arizona tried a quiet fix on one such road back in 2015. A 2023 Geotechnics paper by Chun-Hsing Ho, Jeremy DeGeyter and Dada Zhang followed that fix for five years. Engineers installed a strong mesh called geogrid beneath a Forest Service road near Marshall Lake, south and east of Flagstaff. By 2020, the strengthened sections had no ruts or potholes, but the untreated soil next to them kept getting worse.Why this road needed help The test site was selected for a reason. The road already had deep ruts, and there was proof of failure of another fabric installed in the past. This road provided access to one section of the Arizona Trail, which was closed down by the Forest Service during winter months. Conditions on this road were especially difficult. Flagstaff sits at an elevation of 2,250 metres above sea level. The authors explained that there were around 200 to 250 freeze-thaw cycles annually, along with lots of snow in winter and summer monsoons. The soil beneath was a weak clay with some sand in it. They noted that forest officers have limited budgets. As a result, maintaining unpaved roads was difficult. Geogrids were considered for trial as they would reduce both maintenance and construction costs.What the engineers built The team built four test sections along a 40-metre stretch, each 4.3 metres wide and 10 metres long. The geogrid was inserted between the soil and a layer of aggregate, a gravel-like material used to build roads. Three of the sections had geogrids, one with 15 centimetres of aggregate and two with 30 centimetres, while the fourth had 30 centimetres but no geogrid. The work was done in November 2015, just before a winter storm hit northern Arizona. Next to the four plots, the team left one section of plain native soil as a control. The design software indicated that unreinforced ground required 33 centimetres of aggregate to achieve the target strength, while a section with geogrid required only 15 centimetres. Stiffness testing post-build showed the native soil scored 73.9 megapascals, while the best reinforced section scored as high as 390.7 megapascals. The native soil settled under the test load to 15.77 millimetres instead of 2.1 to 3.5 millimetres in the geogrid sections.What the road looked like five years on By May 2020, no rutting and pothole distress was noted in the reinforced sections. However, the control section had a much different experience. The researchers observed rutting, potholes and cracking in the control section, and these were increasing over time. Moreover, the team drove a sensor-equipped vehicle over all five sections to measure how bumpy each one felt. The untreated soil’s average smoothness score was 0.040 centimetres. The two best sections, 30 centimetres of aggregate with geogrid, gave scores of 0.010 and 0.011. A 15-centimetre geogrid section scored at 0.021, outperforming a 30-centimetre section without geogrid at 0.030.What it proves and what it doesn'tA similar pattern was seen by researchers at Oregon State University on a test road in western Oregon. A 2016 study in the European Journal of Forest Engineering by Erica Kemp, Ben Leshchinsky and Kevin Boston found that geogrid on native soil prior to the placement of aggregate reduced pressure on the soil during loading. It also reduced rutting with well-graded aggregate. Still, the Arizona result is from one road in one place. The Arizona team called for more research on aggregate thickness and drainage. Several backers, including the geogrid supplier, supported the project. So geogrid isn't a cure-all, but in this test, a buried layer helped support the road over the five-year study period.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After losing his eldest son in a 2008 accident, Australian mechanic Gavin Hynam began restoring old cars for young people in need; he had donated at least 19 cars by 2025 and has now received a state honour
articles.summary: For some, grief stays with them for a lifetime.
articles.body: For some, grief stays with them for a lifetime. But for Australian mechanic Gavin Hynam, the loss of his oldest son became the beginning of a mission that has changed the lives of young people all over regional Victoria. The 65-year-old has put his mechanical skills to work for his community, repairing discarded vehicles and handing over the keys to people who can’t afford transportation. Victoria’s 2027 Australian of the Year Local Hero, Bear, affectionately known as Hynam, has been recognized for his extraordinary generosity.Personal tragedy sparks initiative that changes livesHynam’s dedication to community service started after his oldest son, Preston, died in an accident in 2008, just before he turned 21. And after years of grief, the Horsham-based mechanic has found a new lease of life helping young people tackle financial and practical barriers to independence.The idea began in 2017, when Hynam met two refugees who had recently resettled in the Wimmera region, ABC News reports. He was impressed by their resolve to build new lives and knew that dependable transportation could make a huge difference in their opportunities.He used his professional mechanical skills to fix two second-hand cars and gifted them to the young men once they got their driving licenses. He later broadened the initiative to assist other migrants and disadvantaged young people. This became the basis of his Cars 4 Youth program.More than just cars: Restoring old carsAccording to The Weekly Advertiser, Cars 4 Youth enables Hynam to acquire affordable used cars, make any needed repairs and have them road tested before handing them over to the deserving recipients. The donated vehicles also come with six months registration, relieving the burden on the young beneficiaries.By August 2025, Hynam had handed over at least 19 sets of car keys, ABC News reported. The Weekly Advertizer also reported separately on his commitment to the scheme, reporting that at the time of its coverage, 13 vehicles had been gifted.And the effects go beyond transportation. Recipients have been provided with the opportunity to go to university, find jobs, support their families and access vital community services.Helping young drivers gain their independenceAlongside fixing vehicles, Hynam has spent plenty of time mentoring learner drivers through Victoria’s Transport Accident Commission’s L2P program.The initiative matches eligible learner drivers who lack access to a vehicle or supervising driver with volunteer mentors. Participants are guided and practice supervised driving to help them complete the required 120 hours and work toward getting their licences, adds The Weekly Advertiser report.Hynam also volunteers with the Center for Participation’s P21 driving practice program, reports The Weekly Advertiser. His role extends beyond teaching young people to drive, providing them with motivation, practical advice and a caring relationship at a critical time in their lives.Generosity is a community effortThe initiative has also garnered support from those who want to see Hynam’s work continue. Preston’s family came together to organize fundraising efforts in his memory, raising almost $8,000. In December 2024, a Wimmera business group added another $10,000 to the program, the Weekly Advertizer reported. Hynam has also put about $20,000 of his own money into the scheme, according to ABC News.State recognition of an outstanding local heroHynam has been named Victoria’s 2027 Local Hero by the National Australia Day Council for his commitment to helping disadvantaged young people achieve mobility and independence. The Australian of the Year announcement said he would join winners from other states and territories at the national awards ceremony in Canberra on January 25, 2027. His award acknowledges more than cars given. It recognizes how the personal loss of one man spurred years of practical kindness, mentorship and civic engagement.Every restored car is one more young person with the freedom to pursue education, find a job and build a better future, according to Hynam. His work continues to make a difference in the lives of others in memory of Preston.Image Courtesy: ABC News/Tamara ClarkYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Big Issue: Saatchi Gallery exhibition explores magazine's iconic moments
articles.summary: George Michael coming out in a Big Issue interview is among a number of exclusives in its 35-year history.
articles.body:
The most iconic front covers from the past 35 years of the Big Issue have gone on display as part of a new London exhibition exploring street culture.

Established in 1991 to support people experiencing homelessness, the magazine has featured many famous moments such as when George Michael chose an interview with the magazine to come out as gay.

The display forms part of a wider exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery called Beyond The Streets, with works by the likes of drum and bass pioneer Goldie and street artist Shepard Fairey also on show.

Katherine Benson, the gallery's exhibition programming manager, said the covers were a "documentary of our social history and our cultural history".

The Big Issue was set up by Lord Bird and Gordon Riddick to help give people experiencing poverty and homelessness in the UK "a hand up not a handout".

Over its 35-year history, the magazine has featured interviews with everyone from King Charles III and Andy Burnham, to Oasis and Lioness Fara Williams, who went from experiencing homelessness to playing for England.

Describing how the interview with George Michael came about, Lord Bird told BBC London the star "had not talked to the press in nine years" but had then approached the magazine.

"He said, 'look I'm gay and people keep hinting at me and I'm having to hide but I don't want to do that any more - and I've come to the Big Issue because I know you won't distort the story'."

The magazine operates by vendors buying copies for half the cover price and then selling them for the full price, keeping the difference.

More than 110,000 vendors have sold the magazine since 1991, with some 233 million copies sold in the UK in that time.

André Rostant, who has been selling the Big Issue in London for 14 years and whose red tabard is included in the display, said the magazine had provided him with a means to "have cash in your pocket" so you "don't have that thing towards the end of the month where you're skint".

"The thing about the Big Issue is it very clearly states that homelessness isn't helplessness," he added.

"We're doing something about homelessness, we're doing something to keep our situation stable and perhaps improve it."

Beyond The Streets will be on show at the Saatchi Gallery until 5 May 2027.

articles.title: US grounds all flights for hours over tech issues, prompting travel chaos
articles.summary: Officials blame "antiquated equipment" as longest ground stop since 9/11 is expected to have knock-on effects for days.
articles.body:
All flights in the US were grounded for several hours on Friday, causing widespread disruption that is expected to last for days.

No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US due to a problem with air traffic control systems for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) - the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

Officials attributed the issue to outdated equipment and said there was no evidence it had been caused by a cyber-attack.

The ground stop was lifted at 20:15 EST, allowing flights to depart, but it is expected to have a knock-on effect on air travel for days as airlines clear a backlog of flights.

What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if you're affected

More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.

Disruption has continued across the country into Saturday, with hundreds of flights expected to be delayed or cancelled, according to tracker Flightradar24.

The impact of the ground stop rippled around the world, with many US-bound flights ordered not to take-off, including from Europe and Australia's Sydney International Airport.

In the UK, some flights have been cancelled and in-bound flights from the US to Manchester and Heathrow airports are experiencing minor delays.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a news conference on Friday night that the impact of the ground stop would be felt for a few days.

"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," he said.

Duffy stressed that the issue that had caused the ground stop - characterised as "intermittent" instability in communication and radar systems - had not put any lives or flights at risk.

He blamed equipment that was "too old", with overloaded routers producing inconsistent data, and said the system needed a £50bn overhaul.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence that the problem had been caused by a cyber-attack or a rogue artificial intelligence agent.

Both he and Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.

US President Donal Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.

Trump was uncharacteristically silent during the fiasco, however Mullin and Duffy said they were in constant contact with him and he was "fully engaged".

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said it had "thoroughly tested" its systems "to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable" before clearing flights to resume.

Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that he was "not optimistic" about how quickly things were going to get back up and running at airports across the country.

While he acknowledged "antiquated equipment", he said it was unclear why the fault had occurred when it had and that it was a concern ahead of Thanksgiving holiday travel.

"The fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" Pistole added.

A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

A failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system in 2023 prompted a grounding that lasted an hour and 52 minutes, delaying about 9,500 flights and cancelling about 1,300.

"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify of Friday's ground stop.

articles.title: A Queens shopper bought a thrift-store drawing for under $80; an expert authenticated it as an Egon Schiele and estimated it could fetch $100,000–$200,000
articles.summary: A Queens shopper discovers a hidden gem in a thrift store—a drawing authenticated as Egon Schiele's work, estimated to be worth $100,000 to $200,000. Learn about this incredible find and the story behind it.
articles.body: A piece of art purchased from a second-hand store in Queens for under $80 has been identified as the original artwork of the famous Austrian artist, Egon Schiele. According to the buyer, who works as an art handler and is also an ardent art lover, he acquired the artwork from a Habitat ReStore in Woodside, New York. According to The Art Newspaper, the piece of art, which initially looked like an ordinary second-hand item, was later authenticated as an original Egon Schiele drawing. Jane Kallir, director of Galerie St. Etienne, estimated its value at between $100,000 and $200,000, although no confirmed sale was reported. The revelation was made in July 2019, after Kallir, the author of Schiele’s catalogue raisonné, authenticated the drawing. According to WABC, the director of the thrift shop stated that the buyer paid between $10 and $20 for the drawing. However, the buyer told Gothamist that he spent less than $80 for the purchase.The shopper noticed something unusual about the drawingThe anonymous purchaser saw the painting at the Habitat for Humanity ReStore in Woodside, Queens, as per amNY. Being an art handler and art lover part-time, he had some experience with paintings. The drawing interested him because it resembled how he used to draw. Having bought it, he saw some similarities with the drawings by Schiele. He informed Kallir about it in June 2018 and sent her photos of it. However, the photos were very blurry and did not allow her to examine the painting. After nearly a year, he sent her a better photo. Kallir received a lot of enquiries regarding supposed Schiele originals, but in most cases, those were fake. However, this painting was worth considering further.An expert identified it as a previously unknown Schiele drawingAccording to Kallir, a detailed analysis convinced her the work was by Schiele. This black crayon drawing on cream wallpaper, named Reclining Nude Girl, dates back to 1918. The drawing is recognizable due to the fact that it is the girl who served as the model for Schiele in 1918. She posed for him many times in various settings, both alone and with her mother. According to The Art Newspaper, Kallir placed the drawing within a sequence of 22 other known Schiele drawings of the girl. She identified two of them that were probably made in the same modelling session. The features of the drawing itself, along with the depiction of the model, were cited by Kallir as additional confirmation of the authorship.The drawing was estimated to be worth up to $200,000Upon verification of authenticity, the Reclining Nude Girl was displayed in the Manhattan Galerie St. Etienne as one of the pieces in The Art Dealer as Scholar exhibition. Other artists featured in the exhibition include Käthe Kollwitz and Alfred Kubin. According to Kallir, the Schiele drawing could fetch between $100,000 and $200,000. The piece is available for sale and the purchaser promised to donate part of the proceeds to Habitat for Humanity. Nonetheless, reports do not confirm whether the drawing has been sold and the estimated price obtained.Schiele made the drawing in his last year of life. Born in Austria in 1890, he was well known for his expression and somewhat unconventional representation of the human body. He died in Vienna in 1918 at the age of 28, amid the Spanish flu epidemic. The discovery of the work in Queens has brought to light an artwork from the last days of Schiele’s life. It is a drawing that has been lying amongst second-hand items in a thrift shop and has been verified to be an original work of an artist whose works are housed in the great museum collections.You use AI every day. articles.title: Qatar and Turkiye sign a mutual defence pact: What do we know?
articles.summary: Analysts say the pact, agreed amid the US-Iran war, aims to deter attacks rather than build an offensive alliance.
articles.body:
Qatar and Turkiye have welcomed a new mutual defence agreement that commits them to a common position against any external armed attack on either country.

The pact followed Friday’s high-level meeting of the Turkiye-Qatar Supreme Strategic Committee in Istanbul, chaired by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.

It comes as the region deals with the fallout of the United States-Israeli war on Iran and disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz .

So what is in the agreement, and why does it matter now? Here’s what you need to know:

According to a joint communique, the deal aims to strengthen collective defence, promote regional security and establish a common position against external armed attacks targeting either or both countries.

It reflects “not only the commitment of its signatories to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, but also their shared vision of contributing to a more secure and stable regional order”, the statement said.

The two countries agreed to consult one another on security threats and defence policy. They also agreed to expand joint military exercises, defence industry collaboration and personnel training exchanges.

The communique, as reported, did not set out what could trigger the agreement or what form a joint response would take.

Other agreements reached at the meeting covered education, consumer protection, and peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution, Qatar’s Al Raya newspaper said in an editorial on Saturday.

Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the goal is not to form an alliance against any particular country.

Instead, he said, it is meant to raise the cost of any potential aggression so that others are deterred from attempting it.

He said cooperation already rests on an extended military partnership, including a Turkish military presence, joint training and defence manufacturing.

The partnership is moving to a more advanced level, based on converging security doctrines and a shared view of where threats come from and how to deal with them, said Al-Etaibi.

There are fears of a renewed military escalation, pushing states to build up their defences and deterrence, Al-Etaibi said.

The deal comes amid Israel’s aggressive military posture and growing questions over the future reliability of the US security umbrella.

Regional states are looking to new alliances built on deterrence, joint arms manufacturing and less dependence on outside powers.

In the communique, Ankara and Doha said the war on Iran and its regional repercussions must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

They called for “the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz”.

Because supply chains have become a weak point.

Al-Etaibi said disruption to navigation in Hormuz has made it harder to rely on foreign military supply chains.

Producing weapons locally and securing spare parts is now a strategic necessity, not just an economic choice, he said.

Mahjoob Zweiri, an academic and Middle East policy expert, told Al Jazeera that the move to joint manufacturing marks an advanced strategic stage.

Military industries require billions of dollars of investment and long-term commitments, he said, as well as mutual trust over technology transfer. He said the war had shown why countries need their own manufacturing capacity, pointing to Iran, which kept fighting by producing much of its weaponry at home.

The communique also welcomed the Badr memorandum, signed by Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia.

It described the memorandum as a step towards collective defence through “the development of indigenous capabilities”, including joint production, technology development, information sharing and stronger supply chains.

The Supreme Strategic Committee was set up under an agreement signed on December 19, 2014, according to Anadolu. Friday’s meeting was the 12th such forum.

Al Raya described it as a key framework for monitoring agreements and expanding cooperation.

Zweiri said the new pact reflects a high level of trust between Doha and Ankara after a series of political and security tests the relationship has faced since 2014.

The relationship goes well beyond defence.

Turkish contracting companies have carried out 206 projects in Qatar worth $20.8bn, according to the communique.

The two countries also reiterated a target to raise bilateral trade to $5bn and pledged closer cooperation on energy, particularly liquefied natural gas.

On security, they pledged to counter “terrorism in all its forms and manifestations”.

Ozcan Tikit, a foreign affairs analyst at Anadolu, said the partnership combines Turkish industrial and military expertise with Qatari financial and diplomatic strength.

He expects cooperation to expand to missile defence systems, drones, and armoured vehicles, with Qatar possibly joining advanced Turkish air defence projects.

He said several manufacturing projects could also extend to Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

However, he stressed that these were future possibilities, not projects whose details were announced in the agreement.

articles.title: Saltaire's Peace Museum reopens after £400,000 heating revamp
articles.summary: Curator Áine McKenny says staying open all year will allow up to 15,000 more people to visit annually.
articles.body:
The UK's only dedicated peace museum will now be able to open all year round following a £400,000 investment in its heating and air conditioning systems.

The Peace Museum, in Saltaire, will reopen later for the first time since work began in August.

Funded by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, curator Áine McKenny said staying open all year would allow up to 15,000 more people to visit annually.

First opened in 1998 in Piece Hall Yard, in Bradford, the museum moved to Saltaire in 2024.

McKenny said: "For the most part through the year we did very well here.

"But if you've ever visited during the winter then you'll know we got very, very cold without a heating system in here.

"Then also in the summer we went from a freezer to a furnace very quickly because we didn't have any cooling systems either."

She said 21 new radiators and a cooling system would provide "a more stable environment" for the musuem's collection of more than 16,000 artefacts.

McKenny added: "In our first nine months open here we welcomed over 40,000 visitors to the space.

"We can stay open all year round now. We are estimating welcoming 60,000 visitors a year."

Funding for the work was part of the legacy of Bradford UK City of Culture 2025.

Rachel Julian, chair of the museum's board of trustees, said: "This transformational investment represents a strong vote of confidence in our mission and the vital role we play in preserving and sharing the histories of peace and social justice movements.

"As the only accredited museum in the UK dedicated to peace movements, we hold a collection of national importance.

"These works safeguard that heritage and strengthen our ability to share it widely."

articles.title: Fifteen taken to hospital after deliberate fire at Glasgow flats
articles.summary: The four-storey building on Copland Street in Ibrox was evacuated after the blaze broke out on Friday afternoon.
articles.body:
Police are treating a fire at a block of flats in Glasgow as deliberate.

Four fire engines were sent to the four-storey building on Copland Road, in the Ibrox area, just after 17:00 on Friday after reports of a fire on the ground floor.

Firefighters and paramedics initially said they were dealing with "multiple casualties" and police have now confirmed 15 people were taken to hospital as a precaution.

The fire was extinguished and crews left the scene by 22:00.

A section of Paisley Road West was closed while fire crews tackled the blaze.

One image from the scene showed a firefighter up a ladder while at least two residents looked out from a first floor window.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said the building was evacuated and added: "The fire is being treated as wilful and inquiries are ongoing."

articles.title: After 13 years of marriage, a Washington couple divorced and the wife was awarded $328,715, but from her husband's 401(k) rather than cash; an appeals court upheld the split despite her concerns about future taxes
articles.summary: A divorce settlement can look equal on paper but create different financial challenges when one spouse receives retirement savings instead of readily
articles.body: A divorce settlement can look equal on paper but create different financial challenges when one spouse receives retirement savings instead of readily available cash. That issue arose in a Washington divorce case in which a woman was awarded $328,715.53 as an equalisation payment, but the money was to come from her former husband's 401(k) account rather than his cash holdings. She argued that the arrangement could expose her to taxes and early withdrawal penalties if she needed access to the funds before retirement.The dispute reached the Washington Court of Appeals after the woman challenged several parts of the divorce settlement, including the division of marital property, spousal maintenance and attorney's fees. In its October 29, 2026, unpublished opinion in In re Marriage of Goldstein, case number 41005-6-III, available on Justia, the appellate court upheld the trial court's decisions. It concluded that the woman had not demonstrated that the property distribution or the denial of additional financial support amounted to an abuse of discretion.Couple separated after 13 years of marriageDana Leigh Goldstein and Todd Alan Goldstein married in February 2009 and separated in 2022. Following their separation, Dana filed a petition for dissolution of the marriage. After a two-day trial, the court assessed the couple's assets and liabilities and determined that each spouse was entitled to property worth $428,054.19. However, differences in the assets assigned to each party meant that an equalisation payment was necessary to balance the distribution.The court ordered Todd to pay Dana $328,715.53 by transferring a portion of his GM 401(k) account. The settlement also awarded Todd the couple's Bask cash account. Dana objected to receiving the payment through retirement savings. She wanted at least part of the amount to come from the Bask account so she could access liquid funds without having to withdraw money from a retirement account. She also challenged the court's decisions concerning other assets, personal debts, maintenance and legal expenses. After the trial court rejected her request for reconsideration, she appealed.Wife raised concerns about taxes and early withdrawalsDana argued that receiving the equalisation payment through Todd's 401(k) was unfair because withdrawing money from the account could result in taxes and early distribution penalties. She was 59 years old at the time of trial and said she needed financial flexibility rather than having most of the payment tied up in retirement savings.However, the trial court had considered her financial circumstances and testimony about her retirement concerns. It concluded that transferring part of Todd's retirement account was an appropriate way to balance the property distribution. The appeals court agreed. It explained that Washington law requires trial courts to make a just and equitable division of marital and separate property after considering the nature of the assets, the length of the marriage and each spouse's financial circumstances.It also noted that tax consequences can be considered when valuing marital property if they are immediate or directly result from the distribution and are not speculative. In this case, the taxes would arise when Dana eventually withdrew money from the 401(k), rather than directly from the transfer itself. The court therefore found that the possibility of future taxes and penalties did not establish that the settlement was unfair.Court rejected other challenges to the property divisionDana also disputed the calculation of an Athene IRA, arguing that the trial court had incorrectly recorded the community and separate property interests. The appeals court acknowledged that Todd's separate property interest in the Athene IRA had been incorrectly listed as $49,032.92 instead of $55,509. However, the judges found that the error did not affect the calculation of the couple's community property.She further challenged the deduction of $7,909 in personal liabilities from her equalisation payment. The appellate court found that she had not provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the trial court had made an error. Her claims concerning her Merrill 401(k) and IRA accounts were also rejected. The trial court had recognised her premarital contributions as separate property and treated the remaining balances as community property.No additional maintenance or attorney's feesBeyond the property division, Dana sought $1,500 in monthly spousal maintenance for 48 months. She argued that she needed additional support because the settlement did not provide her with enough readily available money. The trial court had considered her financial resources, age, income, living arrangements and the couple's standard of living during the marriage. It noted that she earned $58,000 annually, had purchased a condominium and had approximately $35,000 remaining after furnishing it. The court found that the parties had not maintained a particularly high standard of living and denied her maintenance request.Dana also challenged the denial of attorney's fees, arguing that Todd had significantly greater monthly net income and liquid assets. However, the appeals court found that the trial court had evaluated both parties' financial circumstances and her ability to pay her own legal expenses.Ultimately, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the divorce settlement and rejected her request for appellate fees. The decision left the $328,715.53 equalisation payment through Todd's GM 401(k) intact, along with the trial court's other financial orders.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February
articles.summary: The vote, first expected in 2022, will now be held on February 11, according to the country’s election commission.
articles.body:
South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February, the latest in a series of delays to the long-sought vote, as ethnic and political tensions deepen.

The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year, instead of December 22 this year. It did not give any reason for the decision.

The world’s youngest country, which continues to grapple with violence despite a 2018 peace deal that ended five years of civil war, has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year.

In September, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration. That step allowed the country to move towards elections without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition.

But analysts and watchdogs warned that move dismantled a key power-sharing arrangement, consolidating power in Kiir’s hands and raising the risk of renewed widespread conflict.

“This amounts to a constitutional coup through legislative reforms,” Yasmin Sooka, chair of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, said in October.

“Whether elections take place or not, South Sudan will still need an inclusive political settlement, protection for civilians and institutions capable of preventing further violence,” she added.

Kiir’s government forces and followers of detained former Vice President Riek Machar have been involved in escalating, deadly confrontations in recent months.

Other ethnic tensions and cattle-rustling battles have also complicated the picture in one of the world’s poorest countries.

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, but Kiir’s and Machar’s forces fought a civil war from 2013 to 2018 that killed at least 400,000 people.

Machar has been under house arrest since last March, accused of crimes against humanity.

Thousands mobilised for registration drive

Under the new election timetable, voter registration is due to begin on Saturday, November 14 and continue until November 28.

A 45-day election campaign period will run from December 27 to February 9, followed by a one-day silence period before the February 11 poll.

Gabriel Bol Deng, chairman of the National Elections Commission, said a total of 3,161 registration centres have been set up across the country, with more than 22,000 staff recruited for the operation.

According to the World Bank, about 90 percent of South Sudan’s 15 million inhabitants have no state-recognised identification, complicating their registration.

Such people, particularly in rural areas, will be identified by community leaders and issued an “identification form” enabling them to vote, Deng said.

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia race to build military satellite networks as war rages on
articles.summary: Kyiv seeks to break reliance on Starlink as Moscow develops its own satellite constellation for military communications.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Looking like a tiny desktop tower with wing-like solar panels, the Obria Nano satellite is a small step that could herald a giant leap for Ukraine’s military.

Launched by Himera, a Ukrainian company known for ergonomic military radios, and GomSpace, a Danish small-satellite manufacturer, the first Obria Nano could eventually grow into Kyiv’s own constellation of military satellites, its creators hope.

The nanosatellite marks Ukraine’s “first historical step toward establishing resilient and sovereign satellite communications capabilities,” the company said on October 27, almost four weeks after the Obria Nano had reached orbit.

In mid-October, Kyiv also signed up two Finnish companies, the Nokia telecoms giant and the ICEYE space startup that owns a “self-illuminating” radar technology for obtaining high-resolution satellite imagery in any weather, to look into developing a network of military satellites.

Kyiv’s efforts are rooted in one concern – the nearly total dependence of Ukraine’s military communications on SpaceX, Elon Musk’s satellite communications giant that operates Starlink, a constellation of more than 10,000 low-orbit satellites.

On Thursday, the speeds of Starlink and Starshield, its military component operated by the Pentagon, were limited for Ukraine, leading to “significant disruptions” of their operation along the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Before this, Starlink was also disrupted last month.

Kyiv realises that “it’s possible to create an absolutely new system, but it will take several years,” Anatoly Zak, a US-based space expert, told Al Jazeera. “In the nearest year or two, Starlink and [its military-grade component] Starshield are absolutely necessary.”

Since 2022, Ukraine developed a love-and-hate relationship with Musk, his volatility, shifting loyalties and political demands.

“Musk’s mood swings play a significant role,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “There were times when Musk helped Ukraine, and times of very negative reactions.”

Ukrainians hailed Musk’s decision to provide Starlink services and modems to Ukraine free of charge. The military, hospitals and government agencies operating critical infrastructure quickly made a backbone of their communications.

But in late 2022, Musk refused to activate Starlink coverage in Russia-occupied areas, slowing down or stopping Ukraine’s successful counteroffensive.

The world’s wealthiest man also said that Kyiv should remain “politically neutral” in the future, officially cede Crimea to Moscow and conduct United Nations-supervised referendums on Russia-occupied territories.

“If you want to understand what Russia has done here, come to Ukraine and you will see it all for yourself,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in response. “And then you will tell me how to end this war, who started it and when it can be ended.”

Meanwhile, Russia has reportedly smuggled thousands of Starlink terminals and used them for comms and drone attacks. This February, Musk put an end to the practice by allowing only certified modems to operate in Ukraine.

Kyiv’s attempts to find an alternative to Starlink followed the October 14-24 speed limits for Ukrainian drones imposed without prior warning by Starlink and Starshield.

Drones and drone interceptors moving faster than 60km/h (37mph) lost signal and could no longer reach their targets.

Musk accused the Pentagon of limiting the speed and admitted that the decision was his only after The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had personally authorised the slowdown.

Both Musk and Kyiv realise that Starlink and Starshield are the Ukrainian military’s survival tool.

When it comes to his highly publicised position towards Ukraine, Musk has to balance his own emotional outbursts and the interests of SpaceX, the crown jewel of his business empire that comprises two-fifths of his net worth, analyst Fesenko said.

“If he tries to throw Ukraine under the bus, it may work as very negative advertising for his business, including the Starlink system,” Fesenko said.

Russia’s bid to create military satellites

Another factor is Russian President Vladimir Putin’s calculated flattery towards Musk – on October 28, he called him a “real genius”.

“Putin apparently wants to use the methods he’s used towards [US President Donald] Trump – flattery, unlimited flattery,” Fesenko said.

Putin mentioned Musk while talking about Russia’s attempts to create its own version of Starlink.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it’s very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

The attempts have not been very successful so far.

The military satellites for the upcoming Rassvet (Dawn) constellation turned out to be Qianfan satellites, which are similar to first-generation Starlink satellites and manufactured in China.

Bureau 1440, a Kremlin-controlled space company that runs the Rassvet system, plans to have 900 satellites in orbit by 2035.

In August, the Institute for the Study of War, an international military think tank, claimed that more than a third of Rassvet satellites failed to reach “sustainable operational altitudes”.

By early November, Moscow lost two of the 32 Rassvet 3 satellites launched in the past seven months.

The second satellite that burned in the Earth’s atmosphere on November 1, failed to launch its propulsion to correct its position, according to The Defence Express, a Ukrainian military publication.

Ukraine can also try negotiating a switch to Starlink’s rivals, but they are smaller and less effective.

The US-based Iridium has 66 satellites flying at about 800km (497 miles) above Earth.

OneWeb, operated by the French Eutelsat company, has up to 650 satellites that orbit the Earth at 1,200 kilometres (746 miles). But it is not authorised to be used for military drone strikes.

An average terminal in Ukraine sees five dozen Starlink satellites simultaneously – and only 11 OneWeb satellites. A light, compact Starlink terminal costs up to $500; a much heavier and bulkier OneWeb one costs $9,000.

According to Pavel Luzin, a space and military analyst with the Jamestown Foundation, a think tank in Washington, DC, Kyiv has two options to get its own satellites.

It could work towards heavy and pricey satellites in geosynchronous orbit – or Earth-centred – that could serve for up to 20 years and cover all of Ukraine’s military needs.

Or option two is a focus on launching a system of hundreds of cheaper low-orbit satellites that will need propulsion engines to maintain position, but they will eventually fall down because of contact with the upper atmosphere, and will constantly need to be replaced, he said.

Kyiv can also use much cheaper alternatives such as stratostats or stratospheric drones that serve as “quasi-satellites,” he told Al Jazeera.

A satellite fleet necessary to provide coordinates to long-range drones makes each drone strike pricier, and AI-driven drones that can be “taught” to recognise their targets could bring the price down – and make the satellites unnecessary.

The development of ballistic missiles is another alternative, because they do not need satellite connection but can cause damage equal to the boom from several drones that have gotten through Russia’s air defence system, he said.

“Such decisions are made with all calculations considered, not because Starlink – that depends on current political trends in Washington – needs to be replaced with an alternative,” Luzin said.

“I don’t rule out that Ukraine won’t have to create any alternatives, because SpaceX is definitely interested – even if someone in the company doesn’t realise that – in Ukraine using it further,” he said.

Servicemen of the 68th Oleksa Dovbush Separate Jaeger Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite internet system near the front-line town of Pokrovsk in Donetsk region, Ukraine, on April 10, 2025 [Inna Varenytsia/Reuters]

articles.title: Inside Arab nation's battle against radicalism as top official warns of threat brewing on Europe's streets
articles.summary: A senior United Arab Emirates official warns that European protests have crossed into national security threats, urging coexistence education first.
articles.body: ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — A senior Emirati official is warning that demonstrations in Europe have crossed a line from political expression into a national security threat, arguing that extremism must be confronted before it turns violent. "You can go demonstrate, talk, give a speech, but what [we] saw in the street in 11 cities in Europe is not freedom of speech. It is a threat to national security," Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. The remarks come against a wider European debate over radicalization. On Nov. 3, Europol reported that authorities from 16 countries had referred more than 9,000 links to extremist and terrorist material appearing across 47 social media and gaming platforms. The operation targeted online role-playing content promoting jihadist, far-right, far-left and anarchist violence, including material that could draw minors toward extremist networks. AN IRANIAN REFUGEE'S WARNING TO AMERICAN UNIVERSITIES EMBRACING FOREIGN FUNDING AND RADICALISM What makes the UAE's response distinctive, officials and experts argue, is its belief that the struggle against extremism begins long before police make an arrest — in classrooms, families and the way people of different backgrounds learn to live together. "The root is extremism, not violent extremism. … In our school system, we promote coexistence. We promote the values that bring us together, regardless of our religion, our nationality, our ethnic [background], our color. … We have to learn how to live with our differences and to accept everyone as they are," Al Nuaimi said. Preventing extremism before violence At Hedayah, the Abu Dhabi-based International Center of Excellence for Countering Extremism and Violent Extremism, Fox News Digital spoke with Maqsoud Kruse, chairman of the center's International Steering Board and the UAE foreign minister's envoy for countering extremism and terrorism. Kruse, an organizational psychologist who helped establish Hedayah in 2012, described radicalization as a process that can begin with ideas, develop through emotional responses and, in some cases, lead to violent behavior. Understanding that progression, he argued, creates opportunities to intervene long before violence occurs. "When we talk about countering extremism and terrorism, we understand and realize that no one country, no one institution, no one individual can deal with this on their own," Kruse told Fox News Digital. "We need that international collaboration, that networking, that bridging, where everyone is part of the solution." INSIDE HOLOCAUST MEMORIAL IN HEART OF ARAB WORLD AS FOUNDER REVEALS WHAT CHANGED EVERYTHING Within the UAE, he explained, the emphasis is on an integrated approach that brings together psychology, sociology, education and economics rather than treating extremism solely as a security problem. "That integrated approach means we need to shift from a problem-focused approach to a solution based approach where we create patterns of hope," he said. The distinction is central to the UAE's tolerance strategy: rather than waiting until extremist beliefs turn into violence, Kruse argues that societies must invest in education, community engagement and other preventive measures that address the underlying drivers of radicalization. He also challenged the assumption that poverty alone drives extremism. Wealthy, educated individuals can embrace extremist ideologies, while millions of people living in hardship never do. Kruse pointed to the experiences of former extremists who abandoned radical movements, arguing that their stories demonstrate the possibilities for rehabilitation and reintegration. The institution he leads works with governments, researchers and civil society on prevention programs. Kruse's argument is not that education replaces counterterrorism operations, but that security alone cannot address the ideas and human vulnerabilities that recruiters exploit, and a holistic approach is needed. RESCUE EXPERT WARNS FLYDUBAI HIJACKING ATTEMPT SHOWS US, ALLIES ARE ‘PLAYING CHECKERS’ AGAINST TERROR THREAT Messages of coexistence at the Grand Mosque That philosophy becomes visible in a very different setting across Abu Dhabi: the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque. During a visit to the sprawling white-marble landmark, Fox News Digital passed displays on the approach to the prayer halls emphasizing tolerance, mutual respect and the legacy of the UAE's founding president, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. The messages are difficult to separate from the architecture: bright courtyards, floral inlays and rows of colonnades that draw visitors toward one of the country's most recognizable religious sites. The mosque, with its 82 domes and architectural influences from across the Islamic world, functions as a place of worship and a destination for visitors interested in the country's religious and cultural traditions. ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY WITHDRAWS AWARD FROM MUSLIM CLERIC AFTER PAST OSAMA BIN LADEN PRAISE SURFACES The vision behind the displays predates the UAE's opening to Israel. Sheikh Zayed helped establish the federation in 1971, and the leadership has long presented tolerance as a central part of national identity. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Centre points to religious accommodation and the importance of welcoming people from different cultures as elements of his legacy. The policy became more formal over time. In 2015, the UAE adopted legislation against discrimination and religious hatred. In 2016, it appointed a minister of state for tolerance and launched a national tolerance program. The government updated its legal framework in 2023 to address discrimination, hatred and extremism. Today, the UAE government says the country is home to more than 200 nationalities, a scale of diversity that creates an everyday test of how different cultures and faiths share public space. ITALY’S SCHOOL VEIL BAN EXPOSES EUROPE’S ASSIMILATION FIGHT AS EXPERT WARNS US COULD BE NEXT From interfaith dialogue to the Abraham Accords The UAE has also tried to extend that vision beyond its borders. In February 2019, Pope Francis and Ahmed Al-Tayeb, the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar, signed the Document on Human Fraternity in Abu Dhabi, calling for dialogue and peaceful coexistence. Four years later, the country inaugurated the Abrahamic Family House on Saadiyat Island. Its mosque, church and synagogue occupy separate but equally prominent buildings linked by common spaces intended for learning and conversation. During Fox News Digital's visit to the UAE, the Abrahamic Family House was temporarily closed. Emirati officials told Fox News Digital that the closure followed an Iranian attempt to target the interfaith complex during the war. In Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the B'huth research center, argued that the Emirates' commitment to tolerance cannot simply be credited to oil wealth. "So it is will, not wealth. It's vision, views, and respect to people," Baharoon told Fox News Digital, describing what he sees as a deliberate policy decision to attract people from different countries and give them a stake in the UAE's development. EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT VOTES TO CONFRONT MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, 'ISLAMIST ENTRYISM' IN OVERWHELMING VOTE For Baharoon, the Abraham Accords, brokered during President Donald Trump's first term in 2020, reflected the same thinking on a regional scale. The agreement normalized relations between the UAE and Israel, but he said its ambition went beyond opening embassies. "The Abrahamic Accords are not just normalization," he explained, in his view, the aim was to challenge a pattern in which the Israeli-Palestinian dispute had increasingly been framed as a confrontation between entire religions and peoples. Diplomatic recognition, he argued, matters only if it creates opportunities for relationships that survive disagreements between governments. Al Nuaimi similarly described the accords as an investment in people rather than a bet on any particular Israeli leadership. "We believe in people-to-people diplomacy. We believe that we have to work on the people, build bridges with the people. … Regardless of the government that will be in charge in Israel, … the only solution is to start working on a permanent solution for both sides, where the Israelis and the Palestinians will accept to live as neighbors, will respect each other, [and] will care about the future of each other." He argued that maintaining trust with Israel has also helped the UAE provide humanitarian assistance to Palestinians in Gaza. "Through that trust, we were able to go and help the Palestinians in Gaza. … We have three hospitals, eight bakeries, and we did the infrastructure for the water, and many facilities. … It's because of this relationship with the Israelis." TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION The limits — and the test — of tolerance There is a tension in the Emirati model. Cultural and religious coexistence does not mean the same freedom to challenge the government. Freedom House's 2026 assessment describes a political system in which parties are banned and freedom of expression and assembly are sharply restricted. Its civil liberties record complicates any suggestion that the UAE's system can be transplanted wholesale into European democracies. Still, during reporting in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, the emphasis on coexistence appeared in settings as varied as the Grand Mosque's visitor displays, discussions with counter-extremism specialists and the country's effort to sustain ties with Israel while supporting Palestinians. On Saadiyat Island, the temporarily closed Abrahamic Family House offers a stark image of the challenge. Three places of worship were built to stand beside one another, yet the wider regional conflict has disrupted the setting in which they were intended to bring people together. For Kruse, the answer begins with preventing radicalization at its earliest stages. For Baharoon, it requires political will rather than wealth alone. And for Al Nuaimi, whose warning to Europe opened the debate, it means teaching coexistence at home while seeking a diplomatic future in the region. articles.body: Former Australian MP Rory Amon has been found guilty of raping and indecently assaulting a 13-year-old boy he met through a dating app in 2017, following a retrial at the New South Wales Supreme Court.A 12-member jury returned its verdict on Friday after deliberating for about four hours. Amon, 37, was convicted of sexual intercourse with a child aged between 10 and 14 and indecently assaulting a person under 16.The court heard that Amon connected with the boy through an adult dating app before moving their conversations to Snapchat, where they exchanged messages and explicit photographs. They arranged to meet in July 2017, with the teenager telling his parents he was going for a run.The pair met outside the boy's apartment block and walked through a communal courtyard into an underground car park toilet. Prosecutors told the court that they began kissing before Amon placed the boy's hand on his penis through his tracksuit pants, then pulled down his own clothing and made the teenager perform oral sex.Amon did not dispute that sexual activity took place but maintained that he believed the boy was 17. The complainant said he had told Amon he was 15, although he was actually 13.The teenager told the court he had been lonely when he connected with Amon and was hoping to find a romantic partner. He said he did not fully understand that sexual activity would take place when they met, as he was “developmentally not ready”.Second trial over same encounterThe verdict follows a second trial after the jury in the first proceeding earlier this year failed to reach a decision on two charges relating to the encounter.At the first trial, Amon was acquitted of eight other charges concerning an alleged second meeting with the same teenager. The Crown accepted that the jury was not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the second meeting, during which further sexual activity was alleged to have occurred, had taken place.The jury was unable to reach verdicts on the two charges relating to the first meeting, prompting the Director of Public Prosecutions to seek a retrial.The second trial lasted a week and relied on pre-recorded evidence given by the complainant during the earlier proceedings.The court heard that the boy told several people about the encounter after it happened, including a teacher who made a mandatory report to police. He later learnt Amon's identity after a photograph of the former MP circulated online in around 2020 or 2021. The complainant formally reported the matter to police in 2022, when he was 18.Amon was charged in 2024 and resigned from the NSW parliament in August that year following his arrest. articles.title: How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF
articles.summary: The SAF successes in Kordofan are seeing the battle against the RSF turn in favour of the Sudanese government.
articles.body:
Khartoum, Sudan – The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in west Kordofan this week, shifting the war against the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in its favour.

On Friday, the Sudanese army took control of al-Khuwai, according to local media. This is one of the main towns in West Kordofan and a strategically important site in the army’s ongoing campaign against the RSF in the resource-rich state, which began several weeks ago.

So far, the offensive by the SAF and allied Darfur forces has succeeded in breaking the RSF siege on al-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and surrounding areas.

It has also opened up new routes for the army in central and southwest Sudan, paving the way for significant SAF advances in South Kordofan, all the way to Babnusa and the approaches to North Darfur, including an important road linking al-Nuhud, the site of gold mines, and al-Khuwai.

The RSF, alongside its alleged allies in the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdelaziz Al-Hilu, still holds al-Nuhud and parts of South Kordofan. But its recent defeats in southern and western Sudan could weaken the paramilitary’s ability to coopt tribal groups in the region.

“The RSF’s shift from attack to defence will alter its military composition, which was built on demanding rapid tribal support,” Mohamed Ali, an independent Sudanese analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“The Kordofan region is not a social stronghold for the RSF; therefore, it is expected to withdraw from the region and reposition its forces in Darfur. This would give the army a strategic advantage in Kordofan and could make Darfur the new epicentre of the conflict sooner than expected.”

The RSF’s main social and tribal support base is among the Arab communities of south and east Darfur, including areas around Nyala and el-Daein, along with border areas with neighbouring countries.

The RSF has relied heavily on mobilising tribes and civilians in areas under its control, said Mohiedeen Mohamed, an expert on Sudanese military affairs. This is particularly true when the paramilitary comes under attack from several fronts and reinforcements are desperately needed to hold the line.

But this informal coalition is also vulnerable to the changing circumstances in the war, with a number of tribal and other groups defecting from the RSF in recent weeks, as the SAF gains ground.

“When the RSF expanded into parts of the Kordofan region, it established alliances with certain tribal groups and local communities,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera.

“However, these alliances can be understood, at least in part, as arrangements driven by military and political necessity, rather than necessarily reflecting the longstanding social and historical integration.”

After the downfall of former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir in 2019, a power struggle between General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan , the head of the SAF, and his former ally in the RSF, Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo , emerged, developing into a nationwide conflict between the two sides in April 2023.

Fighting between the SAF and RSF has resulted in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with about 150,000 people killed and more than 14 million of Sudan’s 53 million population displaced in the ongoing war.

Following SAF’s military successes in Khartoum and other areas, fighting has focused on the remote, impoverished but oil-rich and strategically important Sudanese provinces of Darfur and Kordofan.

The recent battles in Kordofan form part of a broader struggle over geography, economic resources, and supply routes connecting Sudan’s central regions with Darfur and beyond.

The RSF still consolidates control across all five states in Darfur, including el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, which fell to the RSF in October 2025 after a brutal siege and bloody reprisals that saw thousands of civilians killed, tortured, detained or raped .

The United Nations has identified Kordofan as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict and said fighting in the area is complicating an already dire humanitarian situation.

Continued fighting has seen about 4.5 million civilians flee to Chad, Egypt, South Sudan, and other neighbouring countries.

Civilians are paying the highest price in the war, with drones targeting them and civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, health facilities, power and water plants.

About 160 people were killed in drone attacks over several days in October in western regions of Sudan.

While both sides have been accused of using drones, analysts see the RSF’s use of drones as part of a wider strategy of intimidation and economic disruption, aimed at spreading fear and paralysing daily life in government areas.

“However, the military balance in Kordofan is shifting. The SAF’s growing air superiority, extensive use of drones, and changing ground tactics have enabled advances along unexpected routes, as demonstrated by the capture of Al-Khuwei,” said Mohamed. “These developments significantly reduce the RSF’s chances of regaining lost territory.”

Most humanitarian assistance operations in the region have halted due to the deteriorated security situation.

Omer Yousif, 55, a driver who works in aid delivery for an organisation called Tasami, said travelling through his native Kordofan has become an increasingly dangerous task. But he believes the humanitarian and security situation might improve if the SAF campaign in the region is successful.

“We were travelling to all of Kordofan region despite the danger because we wanted to help our people. I was captured last August by the militia and I was beaten. Some of my colleagues were tortured and killed,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Restoring the Kordofan region [to the SAF] means more aid can be delivered to both Kordofan and Darfur region.”

Al-Rasheed Mohamed, a military expert, told Al Jazeera the SAF offensive in Kordofan appears to have had some success in consolidating their gains in central Sudan, and opening a new route towards Darfur.

“Of course, the current operations along the western strategic axis are part of a broader military strategy linked to the overall plan to reclaim control of the entire country and restore Sudan’s sovereignty over every inch of its territory,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Although the advances have varied across different fronts, the overarching strategic objective remains the same – the army is now advancing and taking the initiative across these fronts, while the RSF has been pushed into a defensive position.”

Control of Kordofan also brings considerable economic and strategic benefits, with the region being rich in agricultural products, including sesame seeds, groundnuts, hibiscus and gum arabic.

It is also home to the strategically important Heglig oilfield, a major oil processing and transit hub for Sudanese and South Sudanese crude, as well as gold.

“Ultimately, restoring state control and stability across Kordofan is not merely a territorial or security objective; it is a critical economic and national sovereignty priority,” Mohamed al-Nayer, a professor of economics at the University of Sudan, told Al Jazeera.

“It would enable [the] Sudan [government] to regain control of its natural resources, revive exports, restore oil production, increase foreign currency revenues, and lay the foundations for sustainable economic recovery in the short and long term.”

Kordofan’s proximity to South Sudan also gives it control over key border crossings, trade routes, pastoral corridors and critical oil infrastructure.

Whoever controls Kordofan would thus gain significant economic leverage and strategic influence with neighbouring South Sudan.

“Kordofan’s stability is equally important to South Sudan, whose oil exports depend on transportation through Sudanese territory to Bashayer Port,” said al-Nayer.

“Both countries therefore share a strategic interest in securing oil infrastructure, protecting border areas, and restoring cross-border trade.”

Of particular importance are the area’s strategic oil fields, particularly Heglig and Balila in West Kordofan, which produce 90% of Sudan’s oil. Control over these resources also grants the government linked to the SAF added national and international significance and legitimacy.

“Securing these fields and restoring oil production would help reduce Sudan’s dependence on imported petroleum products, strengthen public revenues, and support economic recovery,” alNayer added.

articles.title: Play Sunday or forfeit: Oklahoma AD rips SEC commissioner over controversial Ole Miss FAA scheduling decision
articles.summary: Oklahoma AD Roger Denny says SEC commissioner Greg Sankey forced the Sooners to play Sunday or forfeit after Ole Miss couldn't fly to Norman.
articles.body: BATON ROUGE, La. - The FAA ground stop ended Friday night. The drama in the SEC was just getting started, over scheduling. After a nationwide air travel shutdown left college football teams scrambling to reach their destinations, a bitter dispute erupted over the Oklahoma–Ole Miss game in Norman. FAA GROUND STOP LIFTED ON FRIDAY NIGHT, BUT SOME COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS STILL SCRAMBLING TO TRAVEL From Washington to Tennessee, multiple schools were set to take off on Friday afternoon for their Saturday games, which involved teams getting on their respective charter flights, only to be told they'd have to deplane due to the FAA groundstop. This included the Texas Longhorns, who were scheduled to play LSU on Saturday night here in Baton Rouge. Once the ground stop lifted, some teams managed to get back in the air. Kickoff times shifted where necessary, and schools worked to salvage their Saturday schedules. But Ole Miss remained grounded in Oxford. And Oklahoma wanted answers. Oklahoma and Ole Miss involved in heated situation over scheduling Within the SEC, a battle was brewing between Ole Miss and Oklahoma regarding their scheduled kickoff on Saturday afternoon in Norman. After being forced to deplane Friday, Ole Miss players and staff returned to the football facility to await word on when they could leave for Norman. When the FAA lifted the ground stop, the Rebels prepared to head back to the airport. But another problem emerged: Their charter operator could no longer accommodate a Friday night departure. According to sources, flight crew duty limits were part of the issue, leaving Ole Miss without a crew available to complete the trip that night. Early Saturday morning, the SEC released a statement regarding the situation, which it says also was due to the Rebels not being able to depart Oxford until late Saturday afternoon. "The Ole Miss football team was unable to depart Oxford Friday night due to the FAA ground stoppage," the SEC said in a statement. "After the stoppage was lifted, a late-night departure could not be accommodated by the charter company with which Ole Miss was contracted and the team’s departure has been delayed until Saturday afternoon." That explanation did little to ease the anger in Norman. Sooners blast Greg Sankey over Sunday game or forfeit ultimatum Oklahoma officials wanted the game played Saturday, even if that meant moving kickoff into the evening. During multiple calls with the SEC and Ole Miss on Friday night, the Sooners made their objections clear. According to Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny, it was commissioner Greg Sankey who ultimately made it clear that the decision was final. Denny released a very pointed statement early Saturday morning, pointing out that Sankey told them that it was either play on Sunday or forfeit the game against Ole Miss. "We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution," Oklahoma AD Roger Denny noted. "After multiple conversations with the league office, Commissioner Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit. "Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference's decision tonight." Fans left scrambling as Oklahoma–Ole Miss showdown gets extra juice Texas, Tennessee and others across college football were among the teams able to reach their destinations Friday night, so Ole Miss will face plenty of questions from frustrated Oklahoma fans about why the Rebels couldn't do the same. That comparison alone doesn't establish that Ole Miss had another workable option. To be fair, different charter arrangements and crew availability can produce different outcomes. ARCH MANNING, TEXAS SURVIVE OLE MISS AFTER ANOTHER SECOND-HALF MELTDOWN CREATES AUSTIN ANXIETY But, when an athletic director says that his team was forced to go along with the conference's decision against their will, it's not hard to understand why the Oklahoma football program would feel more than agitated. "I understand that difficult decisions sometimes must be made under extraordinary circumstances," Sooners AD Roger Denny continued. "But those decisions must also consider the impact on everyone involved. Put simply, this decision isn't fair to our athletes, our institution, or to Sooner Nation. "But we've been given no other choice. We are obligated to play the game when directed, but we remain steadfast in our belief that the wrong outcome was reached this evening." I think it's fair to say that Ole Miss and Oklahoma will not be sharing Christmas cards this year, and Saturday's game will have some extra juice to it. As for the rest of this bizarre weekend, I headed down to my Baton Rouge hotel lobby for a bottle of water around 12:30 a.m., only to run into Texas coach Steve Sarkisian and quarterback Arch Manning. An elevator ride with Longhorns defensive coordinator Will Muschamp helped put a bow on a Friday that college football won't soon forget.
