articles.title: THAD ROTHROCK: Bible reminds us to keep serving God even after we retire
articles.summary: Barna Group found only 19% of Christians say their church provides intergenerational connections, yet older adults have decades of wisdom to offer.
articles.body: Culture may see retirement as a time to step back, but Scripture never suggests that our calling retires with us. In fact, the psalmist prayed, "Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, my God, till I declare your power to the next generation, your mighty acts to all who are to come." (Psalm 71:18 NIV) Even in his old age, the psalmist petitioned God for more time on earth to continue living out the calling set before him and to declare the truths of God to the generations who will follow. WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE Contrary to what culture says, one’s role in the community becomes most urgent in his later years. Paul told Titus the same thing and instructed older believers to teach what is good and train those younger than them. Neither the psalmist nor the Apostle Paul considered age as a legitimate reason to pull back; rather, both considered it the qualification for stepping further in. It can be easy to treat retirement from a career as retirement from the church as well, as though stepping down from a job also means stepping away from service. The transition is gentle. A person might move from active participation in ministry to being on its prayer list, from teaching a class to sitting in the back row. JUDGE JUDY CREDITS HER HONOR PROGRAM WITH MAKING HER 'HOPEFUL' FOR THE NEXT GENERATION While the shift away from a lifetime of active service in the community is well-intentioned, treating retirement as a phasing out opposes what Scripture prescribes for older churchgoers, which is to draw even closer to the younger generations. When elder believers draw from deep reservoirs of life experience and Spirit-led sanctification to counsel younger or more immature believers, they’re faithful to the charge by the Apostle Paul to see to it that all can be presented mature in Christ (Colossians 1:28-29). In fact, the church has benefited from and treasured this kind of discipleship for centuries. GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM The practical case follows directly from the theological one. A congregation losing its younger members to another church or to religious disaffiliation may not be because of a lack of programming. It may be that folks leave because of a lack of engaged older mentors. The generation now entering retirement has spent decades leading households, raising children, weathering seasons of doubt and staying in the church through it all. They don’t lack wisdom. They just lack the opportunity to extend it to the rest of the congregation. THE CRISIS FACING AMERICAN BOYS MIGHT TRACE BACK TO ONE ESSENTIAL PROBLEM Barna Group found that 77% of adults 55 and older have a close relationship with someone younger, but only 19% of Christians say their church provides opportunities for people from different generations to connect. Yet, young adults say the top social reason they come to church is to build deeper relationships with other Christians. So, what would it look like for aged wisdom to be championed within a community? EX-PRISONER WHO BECAME MAYOR AND PASTOR CREDITS FAITH-BASED PROGRAM WITH GIVING HIM SECOND CHANCE Senior living communities like ours offer a glimpse of what this can look like lived out. Residents lead the choirs at their life plan communities rather than simply attending them. They volunteer in chaplaincy work alongside our caregivers, sitting with residents who are further along in illness or grief than they are. They chair resident associations and continue serving in leadership roles at their home churches. None of this is unusual for them. It is simply what continues when nobody has told them their season of contribution is over. A congregation losing its younger members to another church or to religious disaffiliation may not be because of a lack of programming. It may be that folks leave because of a lack of engaged older mentors. Congregations bear fruit when they deliberately recognize this opportunity, rather than assume it will happen on its own. Mentorship can be built into structure, rather than left to whoever happens to volunteer. A church that wants its retirees mentoring its twentysomethings will bear new fruit when it asks for it directly, pairs people intentionally and treats that pairing as real ministry work rather than a nice idea. EXCLUSIVE: NEW CHURCH CAMPAIGN SAYS AMERICA'S FAMILY CRISIS WON'T BE SOLVED BY POLITICS, BUT BY PASTORS This can look as simple as an established deacon walking a new one through a hard pastoral visit, or a retired teacher counseling a young couple through their first year of marriage. The alternative — leaving it informal — can easily become the same thing as not asking at all. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Scripture never frames old age as a countdown to irrelevance. It frames it as the season with the most to declare and the least time left to declare it in, which makes this time of life more urgent, not less. The picture of retirement that most congregations envision, a quiet transition into rest and gratitude, was never the biblical picture. Even in the psalmist's telling, old age comes with an assignment, not a discharge from one. The question now becomes: Will the church call on its older members to step into this crucial role?

articles.title: Ben Shapiro warns Democrats have 'strong incentive' to crater the economy and blame Trump
articles.summary: Ben Shapiro warns that Democrats have a strong incentive to crater the American economy after their sweeping midterm wins and blame Trump for it.
articles.body: Democrats could be gearing up to undermine the economy and leave President Donald Trump to shoulder the blame, Daily Wire co-founder Ben Shapiro warned this week, raising concerns about the party's agenda following its 2026 midterm victories. "I think that the Democrats right now have a strong incentive to basically crater the American economy over the course of the next two years and blame President Trump for it," Shapiro told Sean Hannity on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. Shapiro predicted that Democrats would introduce "affordability bills" that "aren't actually about affordability" and seek to "destroy" the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, as part of what he characterized as a broader effort to undermine Trump's presidency. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE "[The AI industry] is responsible for the vast majority of economic growth in the country right now," Shapiro said. articles.title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
articles.summary: Demonstrators armed with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.

The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.

The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".

Innovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".

However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth".

Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk.

Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase.

She is also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it is operational.

Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need.

"At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment.

"The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed."

AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves.

At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW.

But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.

The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.

The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild".

Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all.

"Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."

Friends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres.

She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland.

"These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments.

"There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well.

"The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be."

The Scottish government confirmed it would publish new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and was "developing a strategic approach to maximising the public benefit from data centres located in Scotland"

A spokesperson added: "Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also mandating an Environmental Impact Assessment to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts."

articles.title: Bonnie Tyler remembers loved ones in posthumous Christmas single
articles.summary: Christmas single Love, Light and Peace was Bonnie Tyler's last studio recording, and was released on Friday.
articles.body:
Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday.

The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.

Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace".

The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight."

The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death.

Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts.

The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977.

Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded.

Tyler's husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan, previously said she would have wanted fans to hear the music she was working on, and gave his blessing for the song's release .

Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years .

In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for her at Swansea Minster.

articles.title: ‘Unable to determine probable cause’: Arizona judge releases DUI suspect over AI-generated police report
articles.summary: An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect due to uncertainties in an AI-generated police report, raising questions about the use of artificial intelligence in law enforcement documentation.
articles.body: An Arizona judge has ordered the release of a 37-year-old man accused of driving under the influence after discovering that the arresting officer used an artificial intelligence tool to help prepare the police report.Maricopa Superior Court Judge Daniel Fenzel said he could not establish probable cause because the report did not clarify which parts of the account had been written by the officer and which may have been generated by AI.Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on October 29 after an Arizona Department of Public Safety trooper allegedly spotted his car travelling at 100 miles per hour on Interstate 10 in Phoenix at around 12.33 am.The arrest report stated that the trooper detected the smell of alcohol on Quidera's breath and found several open containers inside the vehicle. It also recorded that he displayed all six indicators of intoxication during field sobriety tests.However, the document included a disclaimer stating: "This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer's own observations and recollections," as cited by ABC News.During Quidera's initial court appearance, Fenzel questioned the extent to which generative AI had contributed to the report."The court is unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI," the judge said."Therefore, the court is unable to determine probable cause at this time."Fenzel clarified that the decision did not prevent prosecutors from pursuing the DUI case at a later stage. Quidera was scheduled to appear for arraignment on Thursday.The Arizona Department of Public Safety confirmed that its officers use Truleo, an AI tool, to assist with drafting police reports.Raul Garcia, who represents the department, said its guidelines allow artificial intelligence to support the preparation of reports but require officers to remain responsible for the final document."Under Department policy, AI tools may be used only as an aid in preparing a report narrative. The trooper remains the author of the report and is responsible for its accuracy and completeness," Garcia said.He added that officers must check the draft against body-worn camera recordings and other available evidence before submitting it. They are also required to verify details such as names, timings, locations and actions, correct inaccuracies and obtain supervisory approval.Garcia said troopers must complete department-approved training before using the technology.The case comes amid wider legal scrutiny of AI-generated material presented in court proceedings in Arizona.In a separate matter, the Arizona Court of Appeals ordered Gabriel Paul Horcasitas to be resentenced following his manslaughter conviction. The decision came after the victim's sister presented an AI-generated video depicting the deceased speaking during the sentencing hearing.In its September 30 ruling, the appeals court found that the trial judge's consideration of the video had prejudiced Horcasitas to such an extent that the sentencing process was fundamentally unfair.You use AI every day.
